title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti hits pause on electrical upgrades tied to a big data center plan—what it means for rates and water.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.

Tonight we're digging into Ypsilanti Township's decision to pause major electrical infrastructure work for six months while it studies a proposed University of Michigan research computing center backed by Los Alamos National Laboratory.
That sounds like a big local move with ripple effects. Graham, what's the story behind this moratorium?
The township board approved the 180-day pause today on new or expanded high-voltage utility facilities. It's directly tied to concerns over that UM project and how it could strain the grid.
Why now? Has this been building for a while?

Residents near proposed sites have been worried about water and power demands for months. Yesterday Washtenaw leaders were pitching a similar data center idea as an economic win with jobs and tax revenue.
So the county sees upside, but the township is hitting the brakes. What exactly are they studying during these 180 days?

Impacts on the regional grid, which is already feeling pressure from AI growth, plus effects on local water supplies and land use. The measure gives the community time to gather data before any approvals.
That makes sense for a place like Ypsilanti Township. How does this fit into the bigger picture across Washtenaw and the state?
It's part of a wave of local pushback. We've seen other townships weighing similar pauses or rules, and this one specifically targets the electrical side that would feed these facilities.
What does a project like this mean for electric bills if it moves forward?
Ratepayers within driving distance would likely foot the bill for any utility upgrades needed to support hundreds of megawatts of new load. That's the reality when big data centers come online.
And water? Michigan residents near these sites keep raising that flag.

Exactly. Aquifers and municipal supplies are already stretched by growth, and data centers can be water-intensive for cooling. Today's other proposal would force operators to disclose exactly how much they're using.
That disclosure bill sounds like it could give communities real leverage. Is it statewide?
Yes, a new state proposal requires reporting on water consumption so towns have the numbers before projects get approved.
Who are the key players here in Ypsilanti? University of Michigan, Los Alamos—what's their role?
The center is a UM research computing facility with Los Alamos National Laboratory backing. It's the kind of high-performance setup that needs serious power and cooling infrastructure.
And the township board is responding to resident input on this. What happens next after the 180 days?
They'll review the study findings and decide whether to lift the pause, add conditions, or make other changes. It could set a precedent for how other communities handle similar proposals.
Meanwhile, Lansing is looking at tax breaks and power rules that could speed things up or slow them down. How does that interact with local pauses like this one?

Lawmakers are reviewing multiple bills on taxes and electricity access. Depending on what passes, projects needing hundreds of megawatts could move faster—or face more hurdles. It affects the whole state.
Residents might see higher utility bills or new local revenue. That's a real trade-off.
Right. And it ties into yesterday's news that the state quietly broadened tax incentives, shielding data centers from most local property taxes for up to 12 years in many places.
Big Rapids and rural counties could lose millions while still dealing with higher electricity and water costs. That seems uneven.
It rewards companies locating here but leaves townships with less leverage to negotiate. That's the tension lawmakers are weighing right now.
Shifting to St. Joseph County—they're drafting noise rules for 24/7 operations. What's the concern there?
Officials are also tracking extra power draw from the regional grid. Residents within 30 miles worry about constant hum and higher electric rates if big loads come online.
Noise ordinances feel like a practical local tool. Any other recent pushback worth noting?
New Buffalo township rejected a permit for a storage yard tied to a data center project. That means fewer construction impacts and truck traffic for Berrien County residents.
Small but meaningful wins for communities. What about Wixom—might they lift their data-center freeze early?
Leaders there are weighing whether to end the moratorium ahead of schedule. Residents could soon face decisions on large power-hungry projects affecting local rates and land use.
And the Campbell coal plant staying open to feed demand—that's a big energy story.

The Department of Energy ordered the J.H. Campbell plant in Ottawa County to keep running due to rising electricity needs from data centers. It means continued emissions and higher costs for western Michigan ratepayers.
That underscores how AI growth is reshaping the grid. Any legal fights bubbling up?
Raeden is suing the state, claiming Michigan's moratorium illegally blocked its $500 million Gibraltar campus in Wayne County. The case could force compensation or lift restrictions.
That lawsuit adds uncertainty for opponents who thought the site was off the table.
Exactly. Local officials and residents now face renewed questions about who controls future development.
Plenty happening across the state. Let's look ahead to meetings listeners can actually attend tonight.
Tonight several townships are taking up data center rules. Springfield Charter Township Planning Commission is discussing proposed zoning ordinance updates.
And the Springfield Township Board has its own data center ordinance discussion on the agenda.
Waterford Township Planning Commission is considering a six-month extension of its data center moratorium.
The Council on Climate Solutions is also meeting to talk about data centers and environmental review.
Those are the key ones happening today—good places to show up and weigh in.
Thanks for laying that out, Graham. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Township Pauses Power Projects as Data Center Concerns Grow
